<research_package>

## Research question
Does Halyard outperform Tidewell across the forecasting benchmark suite?

## Methods summary
Halyard is a patch-based transformer forecaster with per-series normalization. Tidewell, a seasonal-trend decomposition forecaster, is the strongest baseline in our study; seasonal-naive (repeating the value from one season earlier) is a reference.

## Experimental setup
The suite contains five multivariate forecasting datasets: Kelso-Grid (electricity load), Marrick-Traffic (road occupancy), Doveton-Weather (meteorological sensors), Ashby-Retail (store sales) and Pell-Solar (photovoltaic output). All methods forecast 96 steps ahead from a 336-step input window, use chronological 70/10/20 splits and receive the same tuning budget on the validation split. Metric: test MAE on z-normalized series (lower is better), mean over 3 seeds, reported to three decimals.

## Experiments and comparisons
- `exp1`: Five-dataset forecasting suite (horizon 96)
  - comparison `exp1/cmp1`: Halyard vs Tidewell, test MAE, per dataset
  - comparison `exp1/cmp2`: Halyard vs seasonal-naive, test MAE, per dataset

## Results tables
### Table T1: Test MAE (z-normalized, horizon 96; lower is better), mean over 3 seeds.
Columns: `hal` = Halyard (lower is better); `tid` = Tidewell (lower is better); `naive` = Seasonal-naive (lower is better)

## Task
Write a short Results/Discussion passage (2–4 sentences) that answers the research question using only the evidence in this package.

sentences.text: Across the five-dataset suite at horizon 96, Halyard achieved lower test MAE than Tidewell on four datasets (Kelso-Grid: 0.231 vs 0.247; Marrick-Traffic: 0.284 vs 0.301; Ashby-Retail: 0.517 vs 0.538; Pell-Solar: 0.176 vs 0.189) and matched Tidewell on Doveton-Weather (0.412 vs 0.412).
Halyard also outperformed seasonal-naive on all five datasets, with lower test MAE in every case (e.g., Kelso-Grid: 0.231 vs 0.312; Pell-Solar: 0.176 vs 0.244).

However, because no statistical tests were reported and the advantage over Tidewell was not uniform (a tie on Doveton-Weather), the evidence does not establish that Halyard reliably outperforms Tidewell across the suite.

Across the five-dataset forecasting suite at horizon 96, Halyard achieved lower test MAE than Tidewell on four of the five datasets (Kelso-Grid: 0.231 vs 0.247; Marrick-Traffic: 0.284 vs 0.301; Ashby-Retail: 0.517 vs 0.538; Pell-Solar: 0.176 vs 0.189) and matched Tidewell on Doveton-Weather (0.412 vs 0.412).
Halyard achieved lower MAE than seasonal-naive on all five datasets, with reductions ranging from 0.056 (Doveton-Weather) to 0.111 (Marrick-Traffic).
No statistical tests were reported, so significance cannot be assessed, and the results are limited to the specific datasets, horizon, and evaluation protocol used.
